 The Dangerous Car Recall You Can’t Ignore
 Written by 
 Clark Howard 
 | 
 November 5th, 2026 
 Home 
 Cars

-->
 Your vehicle may face a far greater risk of a spontaneous fire than you might expect.
 According to Carfax, there are currently 3.2 million vehicles in the U.S. under active fire-risk recalls . In the automotive industry, these are commonly referred to as “park outside” orders.
 Too often, when drivers receive a recall notice in the mail, the reaction is: “Yeah, I get all these recall letters. I’ll deal with it later.”
 Please hear me on this: This one is real.
 Why Modern Vehicles Are Catching Fire 
 Auto industry experts can only speculate on the full scope of the cause, but the consensus points to the sheer volume of complex electronics packed into modern vehicles.
 When you combine a combustible fuel source like gasoline with faulty or short-circuiting electronics, trouble follows. Worse yet, this doesn’t just happen while driving. You don’t even have to be inside the vehicle. The car can be sitting parked, completely turned off and “sleeping” as far as you know, and it can still spontaneously combust.
 Modern vehicle complexity has created this enhanced hazard. It doesn’t mean every car under a recall will burst into flames tomorrow, but it means the risk is elevated enough that manufacturers and safety regulators are sounding the alarm.
 Advertisement 
 Critical Actions Every Driver Must Take 
 1. If You Have a ‘Park Outside’ Notice, Believe It 
 If your vehicle has an active park-outside order, do not ignore it, and do not park it inside an attached garage or carport.
 If you continue to park indoors, you risk losing your entire home. I have personal friends who experienced this exact nightmare: Their vehicle spontaneously combusted in their garage, burning their house to the ground. They barely escaped with their lives.
 I’m not saying your garage will catch fire tonight, but why take the chance? If you can park outside, away from your home, do so until the repair is completed.
 2. Make the Time to Get the Repair Done 
 Across the country, driver response rates to safety recalls have dropped lower and lower. I understand why:
 We lead busy lives.
 We rely on our cars every day to get to work and transport our families.
 Only certain auto brands offer loaner vehicles while they perform warranty or recall work.
 Because taking a car to the dealership is an inconvenience, people put it off. But an open fire-risk recall is not something to delay.
 The manufacturer did not build a fire hazard intentionally, but the repair is necessary to protect you and your property. You have to make time, schedule the appointment, and accept the temporary inconvenience to resolve the issue.
 How To Check Your Vehicle for Open Recalls 
 It’s good practice to check every car in your household — including vehicles driven by your kids or teenagers — at least once a year. It only takes a couple of minutes to verify your safety status using your 17-character Vehicle Identification Number (VIN):
 NHTSA.gov: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration offers a free, searchable database ( nhtsa.gov/recalls ) where you can enter your VIN to see any uncompleted safety recalls.
 The Center for Auto Safety: If you want an even deeper look or find government databases tricky to navigate, the Center for Auto Safety maintains an extensive database tracking safety complaints, defect investigations, and issues that may extend beyond standard recalls.
 Recall repairs are performed by authorized dealerships free of charge. Don’t let an unread piece of mail put your home or safety on the line—look up your VIN today and schedule any pending fixes.
